frameworks.name: Commitment-First Sales Model
frameworks.definition: Sell the commitment upfront with clear delivery timeline expectations, then execute fulfillment in batches by region, decoupling sales velocity from fulfillment capacity.

claims.text: When sales teams promise unrealistic delivery timelines (e.g., 'next month') and repeatedly push them out, customers cancel despite having the product already in place, because they lose confidence in the seller's truthfulness rather than switching to cheaper alternatives. Alex Hormozi observed this in an electricity-provider sales agency doing $300K/month in revenue with 120-day fulfillment delays; reframing the expectation upfront ('it will take four months') eliminated cancellations.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Unrealistic delivery promises erode buyer confidence and trigger cancellation; transparent timeline expectations anchor buyer psychology and prevent post-sale defection.
bounded_by: Does not apply to instant-fulfillment sales
Does not apply when price is the primary switching driver

claims.text: Sales agencies operating in fulfillment-constrained environments should lead with commitment (signature + banking info) and collect batch deposits before signaling fulfillment readiness, rather than making individual installation promises tied to specific months. This decouples the sales close from fulfillment velocity and allows the sales team to continue selling while the operations team batches installations by region.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Fulfillment is bottlenecked by external provider capacity
Product/service commitment is reversible by buyer decision (not time-locked)
bounded_by: Does not apply to time-sensitive offers where scarcity is the sales lever
Does not apply when batching creates customer fairness concerns (e.g., 'why did they get installed first?')

claims.text: The perceived cancellation problem in a sales funnel is often a sales execution failure (mismanaged expectations, false timelines), not a product/pricing failure. In the electricity provider example, the 40% cancellation rate dropped when the sales pitch changed from month-specific promises to month-range transparency, indicating expectation management was the root issue, not customer willingness-to-pay.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Product/service is already available to customer (not blocked by technical reason)

anchors.region: Vague month-specific promises ('next month', pushed repeatedly)

bounded_by: Does not apply when product quality is genuinely substandard
Does not apply when buyer circumstances change materially (e.g., business closure, relocation)

claims.text: Commitment-first language in sales closes improves buyer confidence when paired with clear timeline expectation. Framing the close as a request for permission ('Will you say yes?') and bundling it with upfront commitment requirements (signature + banking info) creates a psychological anchor that persists through multi-month wait periods, preventing customer defection due to boredom or competing offers.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Buyer already has access to incumbent product/service
claims.mechanism: Upfront commitment (signature + payment info capture) creates psychological ownership; explicit timeline removes uncertainty that drives cancellation anxiety.
bounded_by: Does not apply to impulse purchases
Does not apply when buyer's circumstance is uncertain at time of close

claims.text: Sales agencies scaling from $300K to $1M+ monthly revenue often misdiagnose their growth constraint as fulfillment capacity when the actual constraint is sales process clarity and expectation management. Fixing the sales messaging (transparency, timeline, commitment structure) can unlock $700K/month in incremental revenue without requiring fulfillment partner upgrades.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: External fulfillment partner is the stated bottleneck
Cancellation rates are 20%+ of committed deals

numbers.axis: monthly revenue stage and constraint type

anchors.value: Sales process (messaging/expectations) is the binding constraint, not fulfillment capacity
Achievable via sales process redesign without fulfillment partner changes

bounded_by: Does not apply if fulfillment partner is genuinely unwilling to scale (contract-limited)
Does not apply if product quality issues are driving actual cancellations

examples.text: An electricity-provider sales agency was doing $300K/month in revenue but had a 120-day fulfillment backlog from their external provider. Sales were promising customers installations would be live 'next month' and repeatedly pushing those timelines. The result was ~40% of signed customers canceling, despite already having electricity (the incumbent product). When Alex Hormozi suggested reframing the pitch to say 'It will take four months. You don't have to do anything. Just sign here, and you'll be the first one to get the lower rate,' the cancellation problem disappeared. The sales team was never the capacity problem—mismanaged expectations were.

A competitor company operating in the same electricity-provider space used a different sales model: they committed to the customer upfront, collected banking information, then canvased the region to batch all installations together before calling in the electrician company. This avoided the 120-day wait-period frustration because the sales team had set a single regional batching expectation upfront rather than monthly delivery promises.

practices.text: When managing a sales pipeline with external fulfillment bottlenecks, lead with explicit timeline communication during the close. Do not promise specific months; instead, frame the commitment as a multi-month wait with a clear upfront promise that the buyer will be first in their region once batching begins.

For sales agencies, diagnose high cancellation rates by first checking sales messaging and expectation-setting before blaming the fulfillment partner. Ask: are we setting realistic timelines, and are we communicating them consistently across all sales calls?

Structure sales closes in fulfillment-constrained environments with three elements: (1) explicit multi-month timeline, (2) upfront commitment (signature + banking info), (3) clear regional batching expectation. This decouples sales velocity from fulfillment timing and prevents cancellations driven by expectation mismatches.
